# Lists Web Data Components

React Web Components that already have API connections.

# Overview

This is a monorepo (a single repository that contains multiple projects), made up of front end components and modules.

# Installation

```bash
$ git clone git@gitlab.joltup.com:jolt/lists.git
$ yarn install
```

# Running Docs

```bash
$ yarn start
```

In your browser navigate to [localhost:3000](http://localhost:3001/)

# Usage

Because all of these use GraphQL on Jolt's Shared Schema, you must wrap any part of your application that uses these components in an ApolloProvider

```
import { ApolloProvider } from '@apollo/client';
...

<ApolloProvider client={apolloClient}>
  {*Your App Here*}
</ApolloProvider>
```

## Changelog Versioning

In your first merge request for a change, add a list of proposed changelog items in CHANGELOD.md in the "## [Unreleased]" section at the top.

After your changes have been merged and you push a new version (see Publishing a New Version below), put in another merge request moving your changes from "## [Unreleased]" to a new release version right below that section.

## Publishing a New Version

Publish new versions on master

Publishing a new version will require 4 parts

- Knowing your current version
- Knowing what kind of change your version is considered to be
- pushing the new tagged version
- passing CI

Be sure `lists-web-data-components` is your current working directory

Run `git fetch --all` to ensure you have the most current versions locally.

Run `git describe --tags` to inspect the most current version of your repo. (You'll need this result for later)

As an example, let's say the output of the current version of our published repo is `@joltup/lists-web-data-components@2.1.2`.

Note: To decide what version you should update the repo to, follow semantic versioning as described here https://www.jvandemo.com/a-simple-guide-to-semantic-versioning/

Continuing in our example, and knowing that our current version is `@joltup/lists-web-data-components@2.1.2` from running the previously listed bash command. Let's say for example that we made a backwards compatible bug fix, and we only want to make a minor patch version change. We know we'll want to update from `2.1.2` to `2.1.3`.

Therefore we will run `git tag @joltup/lists-web-data-components@2.1.3` (notice the update version now). Which sets the current repo to have a new version.

Then I would push the update tag version up with git using `git push origin @joltup/lists-web-data-components@2.1.3` (notice again the new version #)

At this point your new version will be passing through the CI server and if it passes, you'll have published a new version.
